transcript: Chapter 28, The Margin. On the 50th day, Torrin Vos woke up warm, indoors on a mattress, and lay still for a long time trying to work out what was wrong. It took him about four minutes. Nothing was wrong. Nobody was on watch. There was no water to do, no rota on a slate, no number of miles waiting at the end of the bed. Somewhere down the corridor, two women were arguing pleasantly about a delivery of soap. He got up and went and stood at the window of the south quarter, with his splinted arm across his chest, and looked out at a made road with a curb on it, and found that he had no idea whatsoever what a person does with a day. Meridian was not a paradise, and nobody there pretended it was. The bath was a shed with four tin tubs in it, and you booked a slot. The food was adequate and dull, and there was enough of it. The lamp in their room worked, and the lamp in the corridor did not, and had not for two years. There was a paper notice about it with four dates on it. The south quarter was eleven rows of long, low buildings that had been a depot's accommodation, and were now somebody's idea of housing. Their allocation was a room with four beds, a table, two chairs, and a window, and Dessa had the Rhoda up on the back of the door inside eleven hours of arriving, because Dessa Cole did not know how to be anywhere without one. Nobody watched them. That was the thing Torrin could never make anybody outside understand afterward when he told it. Nobody followed them, and nobody stood at the end of the row. The line that said where they could and could not go was a line on a map in an office two hundred yards away. It held anyway, because everybody in that quarter knew exactly where it was. They told Rook about his hand on the third morning, and he did not tell anybody for a day and a half. Wick got it out of him at the tubs, which was where anything ever came out of anybody. Then he came and sat down on Torrin's bed and said it flatly, because that was the only way Wick said anything. His fingers don't close. What? The two small ones on the left. He can move them. He can't shut them. Wick had his own hands flat on his knees, still bandaged. That's the axe. That's eleven days of an open arm on a road with a strip of his own shirt round it. They've told him it's done, and it isn't coming back. He's had it since yesterday morning and said nothing to anybody. The strap, said Torrin. That's what I said. Wick's jaw went. He can't do the buckle left-handed anymore. Not on the tight set. He's been doing it against his own chest with his teeth for two days, and he'd have gone on doing it for a year. And, and I've put a tab on it, said Wick Tanner. Leather tab, sewn, two inches, so a man with two fingers can pull it through one-handed. Took me an hour and I did it poorly the first time. He got up. He said thank you. Out loud. In front of Dessa. Sena Vos had a room with a window in it, and a chair by the bed. And on the fiftieth day she made them all come at once. That was how Torrin knew. She had never once in fifty days assembled anybody. She had spent the whole road being carried and being difficult about it, and saying her piece from a cart to whoever happened to be pulling. A woman who sends for all five of you at eleven in the morning has something she intends to say only once. They came. Rook stood. Because Rook stood. Wyke sat on the floor with his back to the wall. Dessa took the chair because Sena pointed at it, and would not be argued with. Torrin sat on the end of the bed. Right, said Sena. I've had it all from the doctor, and I've had it twice, because I made her do it again yesterday with a pencil and a piece of paper so I could see the shape of it. I'm now going to give it to you in one go, and then we are going to talk about something else for the rest of my life. One. I am not going to die this winter. That's the first thing, and it is the enormous thing. I want it said before any of the rest, because the rest sounds worse than it is, and I will not have any of you hearing it in the wrong order. She had her hands folded on the blanket. Five weeks. That was the honest number if we had stopped anywhere on that road. I knew it, and Rook knew it, and neither of us ever said it out loud in front of the children. The doctor says eight years. She says it in the way people say a number they have got from a chart, and not from a person, which is to say it might be four, and it might be twelve. Eight years. I was going to have five weeks, and I'm going to have eight years, and I would like every one of you to sit with that for a moment before I say anything else. Nobody moved. Good, said Senna. Now the price, and I'm going to say it all, and nobody is to make a face. Two. It's a machine. It's a room with three of them in it, down at the end of that corridor, and I've seen it. It's about the size of a dresser, and it makes a noise like a cat. What it does is something to the marrow. She explained it, and I understood about a third, and I'll get the rest in time. Every eleven days I go and sit in a chair for four hours, and it does what it does. Every eleven days. Not for a course. Not for a year. For the whole of the eight years. The room was very quiet. Which means I don't leave, said Senna Vos. That's the actual sentence, and I'd like it said plainly, rather than worked out by everybody later on their own. There is no version of me on a road again. Not to Sallow Creek. Not to see anything. Not for a day. Eleven days is the longest string I've got, and you cannot get anywhere from here and back inside eleven days. I have been to the wind on a boat and up a lock flight in both directions, and I was once an extremely capable person, and this is the last place I am ever going to be. Three, and it's the one you'll all mind most, so I'm doing it last on purpose. It takes the nerves. That's what it costs, and that's what it has always cost. It isn't a mistake anybody's making. The hands go first, and then the feet. Not all at once over the course, over about two years, and it doesn't hurt. She lifted one hand off the blanket and turned it over and looked at it. Not sentimentally. The way a woman looks at a tool she is about to have to do without. I'll move them. I'll keep the use of them for most things. I simply won't feel them. She was very clear that I'd not believe how much of a nuisance that is until it happens. And she was right. Because I don't. And I won't walk by the spring. That's the feet. That's sooner. And it's the part I mind. Torrin heard himself say, then don't do it. He had not meant to. It came out of him in a room with a window in it and sat in the middle of the floor and could not be picked up. Senna looked at him. Torrin Vos, she said. I have been on that road for seven weeks with my family carrying me. Your father is under stones in a rock cut for this. Marta Faust is under stones in a rock cut for this. There is a brick heap on a platform in the middle of eleven miles of drowned water with a boy under it who did the sums on his own at fourteen and got them right. Every single one of you has got a piece of yourself missing for this. And one of you is sitting on my bed with his arm in a board. And you would like me to weigh it. I only meant... I know exactly what you meant and it is the kindest thing anybody has said to me in nine years and I will not have it. Her chin came up half an inch. There was nothing to weigh. She finished telling me the first time on the second morning and I said yes before she had the paper turned round. I did not think about it for one second. I am not going to start now and neither is anybody else in this room. Eight years. A boy of thirteen goes to twenty-one. That is not a price. That is a gift. And I have been given it by five people who had no business affording it. If anybody in here so much as look sorry at me about my hands, I shall be extremely unpleasant. Nobody looked sorry at her. Wick asked from the floor in a completely ordinary voice whether the machine that made a noise like a cat had a name. The number two, said Senna. There's a number one and a number three. The number one is the good one and everybody wants it. There is a woman called Ivy who has had the number one for six years and is not going to give it up. And I have decided that Ivy is my enemy. How old is Ivy? Eighty-one, said Senna Voss with enormous satisfaction, and she plays cards and she cheats. Rook came and found Torrin at the end of the row that afternoon. Walk with me. They went down the length of the south quarter to the inside foot of the bank, where the grass went up twenty-five feet to a flat top with a cinder path on it and a pole every hundred yards, and they stood at the bottom of it. Give me your wrist, said Rook. Rook? I have known since the corridor on the first night. Dessa did not tell me. Nobody told me. I watched you put a card in your pocket without looking at it, and I have been waiting four days for you to bring it to me. You have not. I've run out of patience with both of us. He put two fingers above Torrin's wrist. How much of the room's lit? Nothing. Say a fraction. There isn't one, said Torrin. I've been in about four hundred times. There's no seam and no coal and nothing to blow on. It's a room with the door shut and I can't find the handle. Rook took his fingers off. Agreed, he said. Torrin stood at the foot of a bank and found that he had been braced for something else, and that having it simply confirmed was worse. Is it coming back? I don't know. You've seen... I have seen four people run all the way out. Two of them came back inside a month. One took a year and a half and one never did. Rook did not soften any part of it. I am not going to tell you which one you are because I would be guessing. I have guessed in front of people about this twice in eleven years and been wrong both times. The second one was a boy of sixteen and he believed me. Then say something true. All right. Rook looked up the grass face of the bank. You did not run out because you are small. You ran out because you carried two things with one pair of hands and would not put either of them down. There is no ladder anywhere that has a rung on it for that, and I have told you once already this month what I think of ladders. He turned round. And now I want you to go and do a thing, because you have been standing about this station for four days being a boy with a broken arm, and it does not suit you. There is a room in this place, said Rook, with sixty years of paper in it. You have carried that thing under your shirt since the night you were thirteen. You have asked four people what it is. You asked your father, and he told you the truth, which was that nobody knows. You asked me at a fire in a ruined yard, and I told you the truth, which is that I have a belief about it and cannot prove one word of it and will not sell it to you as anything better. And in fifty days it has never once occurred to you to ask a book. This station kept a depot for forty years before it kept people. It weighed things and wrote down what it weighed and where it came from and where it went. It has never thrown one single page of that away, because that is what places like this are for, and it is the only thing they are better at than anybody else. Go and ask the room. The records office was in the northeast corner of the station in a long building with a north light, and it smelled of paper and cold and a little of mice. The man in it was about sixty-five, and his name was Norbury. When Torrin came in, he was standing on a set of steps doing something to a shelf, and he did not get down for four minutes. You want the depot run, he said, when he finally did. Everybody your age who comes in here wants the depot run. It's because of the ledgers. They look like a thing out of a story. They are almost entirely lists of coal. I want a year, said Torrin. Which one? That's the difficulty, said Torrin. I haven't got one. I've got a shape, and I'd like to give you the shape and then be told what's possible. Norbury came down off the steps. Go on. My family has had a thing for five generations. My father said that, and my father was told it. And I have worked out since that five generations is a number somebody rounded a long time ago. Because I can only actually name three people who had it. My father's grandmother had it. Her father had it before her. Nobody knows past him. My grandmother is 73. She was 12 when a committee sat in a room and made up the kindling ceremony out of nothing. And she has told me that story about 90 times. And she says the ceremony is 61 years old. So I know what 61 years ago looks like from the inside of my own family. And that's the only fixed thing I've got. So I'd like somewhere between 50 and 90 years back. I'd like the part that says what came through this depot going north. And I'd rather start at the far end and come forward. Norbury put his duster down. That, he said, is the first properly framed question anybody has brought into this room in about four years. Sit down. It took them five days. Torrin was in that room every morning from nine and most afternoons. With his arm in a board and his right hand turning pages. And Norbury did the shelves and the ladder and the lifting and told him which runs were in which hand and which four years were missing because of a roof. They went through carriers' manifests. They went through transit dockets and waybridge sheets and a thing called a north road book, which was nine years of consignments in three different hands. Most of it was coal. A great deal of the rest of it was seed, wire, glass, salt, medicine, and one entire quarter in which somebody had moved 4,000 door hinges from one place to another for reasons nobody would ever now know. On the fifth afternoon, Torrin turned a page in a carrier's manifest from 61 years back. In the fourth quarter, going north and stopped. He did not say anything at all for about 11 seconds. Then he said, Mr. Norbury. It was a line in a list. That was the whole of it. One plate. Dark alloy. 240 grams. Nine radial channels. Part cut. Not through. No maker's mark. No assay. No origin declared. Carried loose. Not crated. Consignor declines valuation. And then a name Torrin did not know. And a second name Torrin did not know. And a place name that had been a town and was now a word. And down the outside of the page, in the margin, in a different hand, in pencil that had gone the color of T, somebody had written four lines. Norbury got his glass and read it out. Because Torrin asked him to and could not have done it himself. It is not a curse and it is not a gift. And whoever told you either of those was guessing. It has already saved a world and it has already ended one. It will not do either again. Tell whoever carries it next. Norbury took the glass off the page. There's no signature, he said. There's no date on the margin. The hand isn't the clerk's. I've had that clerk's hand in front of me for five days and it isn't him. And it isn't anybody else in this run. Somebody put that on a page in a carrier's book that was never going to be read by anyone except a man arguing about a weight. Why? Because he had been told to tell whoever carried it next, said Norbury. And he could not find them. So he wrote it down instead. Torrin Voss sat in a records office in the northeast corner of Meridian with his splinted arm on a table and did the only thing he knew how to do with a thing he could not fix. He put it in order. Sixty-one years ago, a plate with nine channels in it went north through a depot, carried loose, not crated, with nobody willing to say what it was worth. Somebody who had touched it before that wrote four lines about it in the margin of a carrier's book, because they had been told to pass it on and could not find anybody to pass it to. And then somewhere in the next few years, a family called Voss got hold of it. And after that, in a room, at a fire, on a road, a person had turned to a thirteen-year-old and said the thing. Three times that Torrin could name. More than three, probably. Nobody had ever counted. And nobody had ever written it down. Because families do not keep books. And every time it was said, it got shorter. It is not a curse, and it is not a gift had come down the line for five handovers, and had arrived in a burnt-over bowl of hill country on the road north, from Sallow Creek, as it's a curse in a gift's coat, which is not a shortening of that sentence. It is the opposite of it. He said that out loud in their room that evening, with all of them there. He said it poorly, then he said it again properly. Nobody spoke for a while. Say the four lines again, said Rook. Torrin said the four lines again. He had had them by heart since the third reading, and he had them at eighty. It has already saved a world, and it has already ended one, said Rook. Yes. Not will. Not might. Has, said Torrin. Both of them passed, and then it says it won't do either again, Wyke said. That's good, isn't it? And looked round at the four faces, and then said that's not good. I don't know what it is, said Rook. Say what you think, said Dessa. I've got nothing worth the saying, and I'm not going to invent one in front of him. Rook had his forearms on his knees. I have carried a belief about that object for eleven years, and I have told him plainly that it is a belief and nothing better. There is not one word in those four lines that touches it either way. Here's what I've actually got, and it is very small. Somebody looked at that thing sixty-one years ago and understood it well enough to be frightened of it in the past tense. Not of what it might do. Of what it had already done, somewhere, to somebody, before it ever came near a depot with a weybridge in it. And then that person did the only useful thing anybody has ever done about anything. They wrote it down. And they wrote it down for a stranger they were never going to meet, in the margin of a book about coal, on the chance that it would still be there in sixty years. He looked up. I have spent eleven years on the road because a company took the records at Homura, and I have never found the second copy. I have asked in nine towns. I have bought four books off four frightened people, and I would buy forty more. Your grandmother is alive because this station keeps paper. There's a line in a book on the level with a boy's name in it, written standing up, by a woman I do not forgive, because she would not have a number where a name could go. So no. I've got no theory about your disk. Rook's voice did not change. But I'll tell you what I think the world actually runs on, and it isn't power. I have got a great deal of power, and it has never once been the thing that mattered. It runs on people who look backward and say what they saw out loud. The summons came the next morning, under the door, in an envelope, which was a thing none of them had seen in years. It was one sheet. Meridian Station, Office of the Registrar. To Marsh E. Voss T. Tanner W. Cold D. South Quarter, Allocation 11 Force. You are invited to attend a joint interview at the Registrar's office. The fourth of the eleventh month, at ten o'clock, concerning... I, the Reserve Ash Recovery on the South Approach, Thurl Orchard, and the account given at intake of how the source was put down. E. A Records Consultation undertaken in the Depot Archive over five days of the past week, and the item to which it relates. Attendance is not compulsory. Torrin read it four times. They know, he said. They know a boy spent five days in their own archive looking for one thing in one year and found it, said Rook, because the man on the ladder writes down who comes in because that is what he is for, and because you asked him a properly framed question and he'd have been derelict not to note it. That's not a trap. That's a filing system. Then why does it say attendance is not compulsory? Rook turned the sheet over, which had nothing on it, and turned it back. Because it isn't, he said. And because they have put it in writing, which means somebody thought about it, which means somebody knew we'd ask. And because a place that had any intention of making you come would not have needed to send a piece of paper. He'd put it down on the table. That's nine days off, he said. And we'll go, all four of us. And we'll tell them the truth about the orchard. Because it is the truth. And because lying to a station with a book is the single stupidest thing a person can do. And nobody says one word about what's under your shirt until you decide to. You'll decide it on your own. Whatever you decide is what the rest of us will say. They did the bread that evening in the room with four beds in it, with the window black and the lamp on that nobody had lit. Senna was in a wheeled chair by the table with a blanket over her knees, which had taken some doing and an argument with a nurse to arrange, and she had her hands folded on it and her chin up. It was station bread. It was ordinary and it was fresh. And there was as much of it as they wanted, which none of them had got used to, and none of them ever entirely did. Dessa cut it with her own knife, poorly, into six. Senna. Thank you, love. Wyke. Me, she said, and took her own. Torrin. She stopped in front of the window with Milo's piece still in her hand. Milo, said Dessa Cole, and put one down on the sill, and turned it a quarter so that the flat side faced the glass and the dark and the whole of the country they had come out of. Then she turned round. And him last. Elias Marsh came and took it out of her hand and ate the whole of it standing up, with two fingers of his left hand that would not close, and a leather tab on his strap that a boy had sewn on poorly the first time. Torrin sat on the end of a bed in a lit room with a piece of bread in his right hand, and his left arm in a board across his chest, and looked at the four of them, and did the thing he did. He counted. He counted. He had not meant to, and he did not fight it. It came up the way it had come up on the bank over the drowned water, and he waited for it to come up wrong. It did not come up wrong. Five, he thought. And one on the sill. He did not have to put it down. And then low and central and slightly behind his breastbone, in a small place he had known about since the evening he turned thirteen and had not been able to find for ten days, something came on. It was not a large feeling. It was not one degree warmer and not one hair larger than it had been at the top of a flight of eight locks, with a hook still on the end of his arm. It did not flicker. It did not flicker. It did not ask him for anything at all. It had simply stopped being a thing that was over, and started being a thing that was... So, It had just started getting married, and stopped being a thing that it had never done. Music
